title: RFID ATTENDANCE SYSTEM Identification
subtitle: Presented monitoring system
desc: Build a smart attendance system that identifies people instantly using RFID tags!
fullDesc: Build a functional RFID-based Attendance System using an MFRC522 RFID reader module coupled with an ESP8266 microcontroller to identify and log attendance in real time. A 16x2 LCD display shows live status and identification results, while a buzzer and LED provide instant audio-visual feedback for each scan, giving a complete low-cost identification and monitoring solution.
author: Nikhil Patil
innovation: A low-cost, student-built RFID attendance and identification system with real-time status display and audio-visual feedback using an ESP8266-based sensor suite.
problemStatement: Manual attendance systems are time-consuming and error-prone, and commercial RFID identification kits are expensive with little scope for student learning and customization.
solutionApproach: Used an MFRC522 RFID reader module connected to an ESP8266 to scan RFID tags and identify individuals in real time. A 16x2 LCD display shows scan status and identification results instantly. A buzzer provides audio confirmation of a successful or failed scan, while an LED indicator shows live system status. The ESP8266 processes all tag data and can log or transmit attendance records over Wi-Fi.

hardwareSpecs.communicationProtocol: SPI (RC522) + Serial UART (9600 baud) + I2C (LCD, optional)

guide: Mount the RC522 RFID reader module, LCD display, LED, and buzzer on a breadboard or custom base
Connect the RC522 SDA, SCK, MOSI, MISO, and RST pins to the ESP8266 SPI pins
Wire the RC522 3.3V and GND pins to the ESP8266 power rails
Connect the 16x2 LCD display to the ESP8266 (via I2C module or direct data pins)
Wire the LED (with resistor) to a free ESP8266 digital pin to indicate scan status
Wire the buzzer to a free ESP8266 digital pin for audio feedback
Connect all jumper wires securely and double-check the SPI wiring
Open Arduino IDE and install the ESP8266 board package along with the MFRC522 and LCD libraries
Paste the provided sketch and update it with your RFID tag UIDs and names
Upload the sketch to the ESP8266
Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud to view scan logs and debug output
Scan an RFID tag near the RC522 reader and verify the LCD shows the identification result
Confirm the LED and buzzer trigger correctly for valid and invalid tag scans
Optionally connect the ESP8266 to Wi-Fi to log attendance records remotely
